title: Variable acceleration
examples: How do I use integration to find the velocity?
What is the relationship between acceleration and velocity?
Can you show an example using vectors?

explain.say: Today we explore variable acceleration using calculus. We know that acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. This means we must use differentiation.

items: Acceleration is rate of change of velocity

explain.say: If we are given acceleration as a function of time, we find velocity by integrating. Integration is the reverse process of differentiation. Think of it as finding the area under the curve.

items: Given acceleration as function of time
Think of it as finding area under curve

explain.say: To find the displacement, we integrate the velocity function. Displacement is the change in position over time. Remember to include the initial conditions.

items: Integrate velocity function to find displacement
Displacement is change in position over time

explain.say: When dealing with multiple dimensions, we use vectors for position, velocity, and acceleration. We must treat each component separately, for example, x and y.

faq.q: If acceleration is given as a function of position, what do I do?
faq.a: You must use the chain rule to relate acceleration to position. This involves differentiating with respect to time using the position variable.
asks: How do I use s instead of t?
What if I have a relationship between a and s?

faq.q: Do I need to worry about units when integrating?
faq.a: Yes, units are very important in mechanics. If acceleration is in meters per second squared, velocity will be in meters per second.
asks: What are the units of displacement?

faq.q: When I integrate, what is the constant of integration?
faq.a: The constant of integration, often called C, represents the initial condition. You use the starting values to solve for this constant.
asks: How do I find the initial velocity?

faq.q: How do I handle vectors in these calculations?
faq.a: You treat the x and y components independently. You find the x-component of velocity using the x-component of acceleration, and so on.
asks: Do I add the components together?
Is it the same for all axes?

faq.q: Can I use the equations from constant acceleration?
faq.a: No, you cannot use the simple constant acceleration equations directly. Calculus is necessary when acceleration changes over time.
asks: Are the old formulas always good?
When do I switch to calculus?

facts: Velocity is the first derivative of displacement with respect to time.
Acceleration is the first derivative of velocity with respect to time.
Displacement is the integral of the velocity function over time.
In vector form, position is often written as a vector function r(t).

quiz.say: If velocity is v(t) = 3t² + 2, what is the acceleration function?
quiz.why: Differentiating 3t squared plus 2 gives 6t. The constant term disappears when differentiating.

wrong.0: This mistake occurs when students forget to apply the power rule correctly to the first term.
wrong.1: This is wrong because it confuses the function itself with its derivative.
wrong.2: This is incorrect because it only considers the derivative of the constant term.

quiz.say: If the position vector is r(t) = 4t + 3t² in meters, what is the velocity vector?
quiz.why: Velocity is the derivative of position. Differentiating 4t gives 4, and differentiating 3t squared gives 6t.

wrong.0: This is wrong because it incorrectly integrates the position function instead of differentiating it.
wrong.1: This mistake suggests that only the first term is differentiated correctly.
wrong.3: This mistake happens when students incorrectly differentiate 3t squared as 3t.
